<reason>PRO won by making the decisive clash the motion's own language: does access depend on work status? CON's defense of employer financing leaned on Germany/Switzerland, but PRO showed those systems keep the floor in place only because the state guarantees it through mandates, subsidies, and unemployment-funded contributions — i.e., they untie access from work, which is what the motion targets. CON's "unfalsifiable" charge in Q1 was answered cleanly (the US is the paradigm CON-side system), and CON's A1 was essentially "many buyers plus a public net," which PRO's floor/net closing turned into a concession; CON even granted in [A4.7] that the floor must be guaranteed. CON's best live route — Canadian queues, monopsony, recession-scale budget cuts — was genuinely strong and its "visible for decades and still there" reply to PRO's democratic-accountability answer landed. But PRO's invisible-queue point and the observation that both systems fall back on the public budget in a recession blunted enough of it, and CON's queue examples (hips, cataracts) sit awkwardly with a motion about basic coverage. CON also had its final rebuttal clipped. PRO overstated by saying its questions "went unanswered" before CON had spoken, a minor sloppiness. Net: clear but competitive PRO win.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>PRO's [B2.1]/[B3.1]/[B5.2] sequence turning CON's Germany example and stack of tax-funded patches (subsidized continuation, capped cost-sharing, public backstops) into evidence that CON's system works only insofar as the state detaches coverage from employment — culminating in CON's own concession that the floor must be guaranteed.</best_rebuttal>
